title: Itinerary Planning and Tour Packaging (Module 6A, lesson 22)
summary: An itinerary is a plan of a journey showing the route and the places to be visited: a day-by-day schedule showing origin, destination, halts, accommodation, mode of travel, activities and services. For a package tour it is a selling point and decides the package quality; it is printed in the brochure after expert clearance. Types by responsibility: tourist's itinerary (the reference; tour operators must follow it and change it only for safety), tour manager's itinerary (full details including alternative arrangements, contacts, rates), escort or guide's itinerary, vendor's itinerary (so hotels can prepare, e.g. a welcome event) and coach driver's itinerary (pick-up points, timings, parking). By need: GIT, FIT, tailor-made and special-interest itineraries.

Steps in planning an itinerary: research other tours, name the tour, map duration, frequency and departure point, list major locations and highlights, research content and commentary, list third-party activities, fees and inclusions, obtain permissions for private and public properties and restricted areas, perfect the timing and test-drive the itinerary. Background information needed: duration, minimum time per city, purpose, cities, mode of intercity travel, special fares, hotels, first arrival and last departure airports, restricted-area permits and best season. Do's: all halts with date and time, hotel and vehicle names, meal plans, maps, local-language names, unique local information. Don'ts: too many details, ambiguous directions, ignoring the nature of the group, over-recommending hotels, unregistered shops or restricted areas without permits.
A GIT itinerary is fixed (services are pre-booked, so no change); a FIT itinerary is flexible and can be changed on request but costs more.

A package tour sells transport, accommodation and other services as a single all-inclusive price, usually cheaper than buying each item. It saves time and money for tourists and helps suppliers balance demand. Types: escorted tour (a trained escort or guide accompanies the group), independent tour (tourists choose components; costlier), hosted tour (handled by a ground operator on behalf of the wholesaler), incentive tour (paid by a firm for employees as a reward, e.g. a team's week-long trip to Singapore) and freedom tour (the tourist selects services and plans the tour).

Luxury rail packages began with the Palace on Wheels in 1982: seven nights and eight days covering the Taj, Jaisalmer's dunes, the 'romanticism' of Udaipur, Jaipur, Ranthambore and Delhi. Other luxury trains: Maharajas' Express, The Indian Maharaja, Deccan Odyssey and the Golden Chariot.

Package elements: accommodation (primary: star hotels, resorts; supplementary: lodges, homestays, guest houses), attractions and sightseeing (the backbone; the most exciting last), transportation (air, rail with Indrail, Eurail and Amtrak passes, ships and ferries, buses), ground services (coaches, cabs, guides, interpreters, car rentals), events and activities, and insurance. Monsoon packages in the Western Ghats (Agumbe, Coorg, Munnar, Ooty, Mahabaleshwar) show how a season can be a selling point.

GIT groups share a common affiliation (club or business), travel on a fixed itinerary at lower cost through bulk buying (short-halt for MICE and long-halt for leisure). FIT packages are customised for individual travellers who avoid group schedules but prepay transport, transfers, lodging and sightseeing; those who travel in their home country are Domestic Independent Travellers (DITs).

Steps: market research, prepare an itinerary, identification (mode, hotels, dates, capacity), contracts with principal service providers, costing and mark-up, tour brochure, marketing and documentation. A brochure should be visually appealing, concise, honest and comparable with others; tips: white space, simple fonts, clear headings, 'hero' images, clear maps, full details of prices, times and contacts, and space for the agent's stamp; the top third matters most. A tour voucher is proof of payment given to suppliers, who submit it with an invoice for payment after the service. Docketing means putting all the tour documents (receipt, vouchers, tickets, itinerary, brochure, terms) in a bag or wallet for each tourist. Tour programming adds activities (angling, trekking, cooking, dancing, festivals) to make a package more appealing and bring professionalism and value for money.

objective: Fill in the blanks. (a) The Palace on Wheels was launched in ________. (b) The Palace on Wheels package typically lasts ________ nights and eight days.
Identify True or False. (a) A GIT itinerary leaves enough room for modification. (b) A FIT itinerary is flexible but costs more.
(a) False: a GIT itinerary is fixed. (b) True.
Fill in the blanks. (a) A tour in which a firm pays for its employees as a reward is an ________ tour. (b) ________ in package tours means putting all tour documents in a wallet for each tourist.

Match Column A with Column B. A: (a) Escorted tour (b) Hosted tour. B: (i) Handled by a ground operator on behalf of a wholesaler (ii) A trained guide accompanies the group (iii) Paid by a firm for its staff.
vsa: What is an itinerary? State its use.
An itinerary is a plan of a journey showing the route, places, halts, accommodation and activities. It is a reference for the tourist and a selling point of a package.
Name any four types of package tours.
Escorted tour, independent tour, hosted tour and incentive tour (also freedom tour).
It is proof of payment made in advance by the client. The supplier accepts it and sends it to the tour operator with an invoice after providing the service.
What are the benefits of tour programming?
It adds value to the package and makes it more appealing. It opens opportunities for local service providers and meets varied demands.
sa: Examine any three types of package tours.

(i) Escorted tour: a trained escort or guide accompanies the group and helps at every stage. (ii) Independent tour: tourists choose the components, so it is flexible but costlier. (iii) Incentive tour: a firm pays for its employees as a reward, e.g. a trip to Singapore.
Examine the elements of package tours.

(i) Transportation (air, rail, ship, bus) and accommodation (hotels, resorts, homestays). (ii) Attractions and sightseeing, ground services and guides, and events and activities. (iii) Insurance cover; a profit margin is added to get the price.
Elaborate on the meaning, importance and types of tour itinerary.

(i) An itinerary is a day-by-day plan of the route, halts, accommodation and activities. (ii) It is important because it decides the package quality and sells the package. (iii) Types include the tourist's, tour manager's, escort's, vendor's and coach driver's itineraries; also GIT, FIT, tailor-made and special-interest itineraries.
Distinguish between GIT and FIT itineraries (three points).

(i) GIT follows a fixed itinerary; FIT is flexible. (ii) GIT is cheaper through bulk buying; FIT costs more for the flexibility. (iii) GIT groups share a common affiliation; FIT suits independent travellers who want personal choices.
Explain the do's of itinerary preparation (three points).

(i) Add all places of halt with date and time and the hotel and vehicle names. (ii) Include meal plans, maps and brief summaries of the sights. (iii) Provide local-language names and unique information about the destination.
la: Explain the package tour formulation process, in six points.

(i) Market research of the economy, demand, consumer profile and competitors. (ii) Prepare an itinerary with exciting places and events. (iii) Identify mode of travel, hotels, destinations and dates. (iv) Sign contracts with principal service providers. (v) Cost the package and add a mark-up for the price. (vi) Design a brochure, market the package and prepare the documentation (itinerary, vouchers, tickets).
Explain the steps in developing a tour itinerary, in six points.

(i) Research other tours and name your tour. (ii) Map out duration, frequency and departure point. (iii) List the major locations and highlights. (iv) Research the content and list third-party activities and fees. (v) Obtain permission to access private and public properties. (vi) Perfect the timing and test-drive the itinerary.
